Spatial Disaggregation Modeling with R-INLA for Air Pollution Applications

Spatial data are often available at aggregated scales due to sampling costs or privacy constraints, as commonly seen in air pollution information. This limits the ability to detect fine-scale spatial patterns that are important for environmental assessment and policy. Spatial disaggregation methods address this issue by recovering high-resolution fields from aggregated observations. A common modeling approach for spatial disaggregation assumes an underlying latent Gaussian field representing the true continuous process, linked to aggregated observations via an observation model. Bayesian inference provides a natural framework for fitting these models, but standard Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods can be computationally demanding. As an efficient alternative, the stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) and integrated nested Laplace approximations (INLA) approaches offer fast approximate inference. Here, we demonstrate how to perform spatial disaggregation using the R-INLA package. Using an air pollution application, we show how to obtain high-resolution estimates, and illustrate the use of R packages for spatial data handling and processing.

Fernando Rodriguez Avellaneda https://linkedin.com/in/fr-avellaneda (King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST)) , Paula Moraga https://www.paulamoraga.com/ (King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST))
2026-04-28

1 Introduction

Spatial data are common in fields such as environmental science, epidemiology, and ecology, but are often available in aggregated form due to reporting practices and privacy constraints. For example, disease cases may be reported at administrative levels, and environmental indicators such as air pollution levels are often averaged over coarser regions. While such aggregated data are widely used and often necessary for practical and ethical reasons, they can mask fine-scale spatial variation that is important for scientific analysis and decision-making.

Spatial disaggregation methods aim to address this limitation by recovering local patterns from aggregated observations. A common modeling approach for spatial disaggregation assumes an underlying continuous latent process and links areal observations to it through a change-of-support operator, which allows prediction on finer grids (Fuentes and Raftery 2005). Bayesian inference provides a natural framework for fitting these models, but standard Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) (Metropolis et al. 1953; Hastings 1970) methods can be computationally demanding (Tanaka et al. 2019; Yousefi et al. 2019).

The R package disaggregation provides a streamlined workflow for Bayesian spatial disaggregation regression implemented in Template Model Builder (TMB) (Kristensen et al. 2016; Monnahan and Kristensen 2018). Inference is based on a Laplace approximation, which in one example took about 85 seconds, compared with about 56 hours for a full MCMC alternative via tmbstan (Nandi et al. 2023).

The Laplace approximation is faster than MCMC, but this speed comes at a cost. The results can be biased, and the uncertainty may not be well quantified, which is difficult to detect without also fitting the model with MCMC. For example, Fong et al. (2010) found that INLA performed well in most of the generalized linear mixed models they studied, but not in one example with binary data with few or no replications, a problem later addressed by Ferkingstad and Rue (2015). In our case, the likelihood is Gaussian and the aggregation is a linear function of the latent field. Therefore, given the hyperparameters, the posterior distribution of the latent field is exactly Gaussian, and the approximation error comes mainly from the numerical integration over the few hyperparameters and from the SPDE discretization on the mesh. We do not compare our results with a full MCMC fit in this paper.

In this paper, we demonstrate how to perform disaggregation modeling using the stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) and integrated nested Laplace approximations (INLA) approaches (Rue et al. 2009; Lindgren et al. 2011). The SPDE formulation represents the latent field on a triangulated mesh as a Gaussian Markov random field. Aggregation is accounted for through a sparse projection matrix that links the mesh representation to the observation supports. Covariates are incorporated at the fine scale, allowing the model to capture local variation using high-resolution information. After inference, predictions together with measures of uncertainty can be obtained on a fine grid.

Here, we demonstrate how to implement spatial disaggregation with the INLA package using an air pollution application. Air pollution is a major public health concern. Recent estimates from the State of Global Air 2025 report suggest that air pollution contributed to 7.9 million deaths worldwide in 2023, highlighting it as one of the leading environmental risk factors for death (Health Effects Institute 2025). Long term exposure to PM2.5 has been consistently associated with increased all cause mortality and with diseases such as respiratory infections, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, ischemic heart disease, lung cancer, and stroke (Cohen et al. 2017; Burnett et al. 2018).

Despite their importance, many air quality products are only available on coarse spatial or spatio-temporal supports such as CAMS reanalysis products (Inness et al. 2019). This can hide local variation and make it difficult to identify small areas with high concentrations. Disaggregation models address this problem by assuming an underlying latent process at a finer scale and linking it to aggregated observations through an aggregation operator, while providing uncertainty quantification and allowing the inclusion of high-resolution covariates.

Here, we focus on a practical R workflow based on the models developed in (Moraga et al. 2017) to produce higher-resolution estimates of air pollution. Specifically, we disaggregate PM2.5 concentrations in Portugal from the CAMS grid to a finer resolution, downscaling from 0.1\(^\circ\) to 0.02\(^\circ\), which corresponds approximately to a change from 10 km to 2 km. Although our application deals with air pollution data, the same workflow can be used in many other fields where data are observed on coarse supports but decisions require finer-scale estimates (Gómez-Rubio and Palmí-Perales 2019; Forlani et al. 2020).

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we summarize the main disaggregation framework and how it is implemented in R-INLA. Then, in Section 3, we present an example of spatial disaggregation of PM2.5 in Portugal. Finally, we present a conclusions section, summarizing practical takeaways and possible extensions.

2 Methodology

In this section, we present the spatial disaggregation model and its implementation using INLA.

2.1 Spatial disaggregation model

Let \(R \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2\) denote the study region, and let \(Y_i\) denote the observations in spatial regions \(R_i \subseteq R\), \(i=1,\ldots,N\). We assume that underlying these observations there is a continuous latent spatial field that is observed only at an aggregated resolution. This latent continuous model can be expressed as a combination of fixed and random effects as

\[\begin{equation} \begin{aligned} y(\mathbf{s}) &= \boldsymbol{\beta}^\top \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{s}) + z(\mathbf{s}) \\ &= \begin{bmatrix} \beta_0 & \beta_1 & \cdots & \beta_p \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ x_1(\mathbf{s}) \\ \vdots \\ x_p(\mathbf{s}) \end{bmatrix} + z(\mathbf{s}), \end{aligned} \tag{1} \end{equation}\] where \(\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{s})\) represents the \(p\) fixed effects (including the intercept \(\beta_0\)), and \(z(\mathbf{s})\) denotes a spatial Gaussian process.

From the continuous spatial process \(y(\mathbf{s})\), we define an aggregated process over each region \(R_i\) as

\[\begin{equation} z(R_i) = \frac{1}{|R_i|}\int_{R_i} z(\mathbf{s}) \mathrm{d}\mathbf{s}, \tag{2} \end{equation}\] with \(|R_i| = \int_{R_i} \mathrm{d}\mathbf{s}\). We then assume that the observed values arise from the aggregation of the continuous latent process together with a measurement error term. In this case, Equation (1) aggregates to the discrete process

\[\begin{equation} y(R_i) = \boldsymbol{\beta}^\top \mathbf{X}(R_i) + z(R_i) + v_i, \tag{3} \end{equation}\] where \(\mathbf{X}(R_i)\) represents the average covariates over the spatial region \(R_i\), \(z(R_i)\) is the aggregated process defined in Equation (2), and \(v_i\) is an unstructured noise term, modeled as \(v_i \sim \mathrm{N}(0, \sigma^2_{\epsilon})\).

2.2 Spatial structure of the spatial Gaussian process

The spatial random effect \(z(\mathbf{s})\) in Equation (1) is modeled as a zero-mean Gaussian process with Matérn spatial dependence (Matérn 1960). For two locations \(\mathbf{s}_i\) and \(\mathbf{s}_k\), we assume the Matérn covariance

\[\begin{equation} \text{Cov}(z(\mathbf{s}_i), z(\mathbf{s}_k)) = \frac{\sigma^{2}}{2^{\nu-1}\Gamma(\nu)} \left(\kappa\left\|\mathbf{s}_i-\mathbf{s}_k\right\|\right)^{\nu} K_{\nu}\left(\kappa\left\|\mathbf{s}_i-\mathbf{s}_k\right\|\right), \tag{4} \end{equation}\]

where \(\sigma^{2}\) is the marginal variance, \(K_{\nu}(\cdot)\) is the modified Bessel function of the second kind, and \(\nu>0\) controls the smoothness of the field. In practice, \(\nu\) is often fixed for stability. The parameter \(\kappa>0\) controls the spatial range, and a common practical definition is \(\rho = \sqrt{8\nu}/\kappa\). This Matérn specification is also convenient for computation, since it has a direct SPDE representation that can be implemented efficiently on a triangulated mesh within the INLA framework.

2.3 Implementation of spatial disaggregation with INLA-SPDE

Inference is performed using the SPDE approach implemented in INLA. As described in Section 2.2, we assume a Matérn covariance structure for the spatial random effect \(z(\mathbf{s})\). The main idea is that a Matérn Gaussian process can be represented as the stationary solution of an SPDE (Whittle 1963).

A Matérn Gaussian random field can be characterized through the SPDE \[\begin{equation} \left(\kappa^2-\Delta\right)^{\alpha / 2}\big(\tau\,z(\mathbf{s})\big)=\vartheta(\mathbf{s}), \tag{5} \end{equation}\] where \(\vartheta(\mathbf{s})\) is spatial white noise, \(\alpha\) controls smoothness (with \(\nu=\alpha-d/2\), where \(d=2\) is the dimension of the domain, so \(\nu=\alpha-1\); in this tutorial we fix \(\alpha=2\), so \(\nu=1\)), and \((\kappa,\tau)\) control the range and marginal variance of the field. The SPDE representation is convenient because INLA approximates \(z(\mathbf{s})\) on a triangulated mesh, leading to a Gaussian Markov random field with a sparse precision matrix and fast inference (Rue et al. 2009).

Let \(\{\mathbf{s}^*_k\}_{k=1}^G\) be the mesh vertices and \(\{\psi_k(\mathbf{s})\}\) the associated piecewise linear basis functions. The latent field is approximated by \[\begin{equation} z(\mathbf{s}) \approx \sum_{k=1}^{G}\psi_k(\mathbf{s})\,z_k, \tag{6} \end{equation}\] where \(z_k\) are Gaussian weights defined on the mesh nodes. In disaggregation models we do not observe \(z(\mathbf{s})\) directly. Instead, the data are available as spatial averages over regions \(R_i\). Following (Moraga et al. 2017), the key step is to link the areal quantity \(z(R_i)=\frac{1}{|R_i|}\int_{R_i}z(\mathbf{s})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{s}\) to the mesh representation. Substituting Equation (6) into this average gives the core approximation \[\begin{align} \begin{split} z(R_i) &= \frac{1}{|R_i|}\int_{R_i} z(\mathbf{s})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{s} \approx \frac{1}{|R_i|}\int_{R_i} \sum_{k=1}^{G} \psi_k(\mathbf{s})\,z_k \,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{s} \\ &= \frac{1}{|R_i|}\sum_{k=1}^{G}\left(\int_{R_i} \psi_k(\mathbf{s})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{s}\right)z_k \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^{G} A_{ik}\,z_k, \qquad \text{with}\qquad A_{ik}=\frac{1}{|R_i|}\int_{R_i} \psi_k(\mathbf{s})\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf{s}. \end{split} \tag{7} \end{align}\] The matrix \(\mathbf{A}=(A_{ik})\) is the projection (aggregation) matrix that maps the latent field from the mesh nodes to the areal supports. By construction, \(A_{ik}\ge 0\) and each row sums to one, \(\sum_k A_{ik}=1\). We approximate the integral in \(A_{ik}\) numerically: we place a regular grid of points in each region \(R_i\), compute the contribution of each point to the mesh nodes, and average these contributions for each node. Figure (1) illustrates this idea for a region \(R_i\) given by one input cell, overlaid with a triangular mesh, using a \(20 \times 20\) grid of points.

Each grid point lies in one triangle, and the values it gives to the three nodes of that triangle are its barycentric coordinates in the triangle, which sum to one. In panel (a), the blue point gives 0.49 to the marked node and 0.22 and 0.29 to the other two nodes. Repeating this for every point gives the individual contribution values in panel (b), which are largest close to the node and zero at points in triangles that do not touch it. In this example, 230 of the 400 points have a positive value for the marked node, and their values sum to 82.9. The weight of the node is the average over all 400 points, so \(A_{ik} \approx 82.9/400 = 0.207\). Only the nodes of triangles that overlap \(R_i\) have a positive weight, and these include nodes outside \(R_i\). All other nodes have \(A_{ik}=0\), so \(\mathbf{A}\) is sparse.

Figure 1: Example of a region \(R_i\) given by one input cell, shown in UTM coordinates and overlaid on a triangulated mesh, with one mesh node \(k\) marked by a white circle. (a) Contribution of one grid point (blue) to the three nodes of its triangle, with the contribution to node \(k\) in bold. (b) Contributions of the 400 grid points to node \(k\), with zero contributions in gray. Their average is the weight \(A_{ik} \approx 0.207\).

In INLA, these mappings are implemented by defining the SPDE model on the mesh and supplying the projection matrices in the inla.stack() objects for estimation and prediction.

2.4 INLA essentials: installation and main workflow

Before running the examples in this paper, we need to install INLA and a small set of supporting packages for handling rasters, vector geometries, and meshes. Note that INLA is installed from the INLA repository (not from CRAN).

# Install INLA from the INLA repository (not CRAN)
install.packages(
  "INLA",
  repos = c(getOption("repos"), INLA = "https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/stable"),
  dependencies = TRUE
)

# Quick check
library(INLA)
inla.version()

The function inla.version() reports the installed version of INLA, which we use to check the installation. We used R 4.6.0, INLA 26.8.7, fmesher 0.8.0, terra 1.9.34, sf 1.1.1, exactextractr 0.10.1 and ggplot2 4.0.3.

Once the data and covariates are ready, the INLA workflow in this paper follows a fairly standard sequence. First, we build a triangulated mesh to represent the latent field with the SPDE approach. In our examples, the mesh is constructed over the study region using functions such as fm_hexagon_lattice(), fm_extensions() and fm_mesh_2d() (from fmesher), choosing parameters like edge_len and max.edge so the mesh is finer than the original data support.

Next, we define prediction locations on the target resolution, using helpers such as st_make_grid() and fm_pixels(). Finally, for both estimation and prediction, the covariates must be available on the same supports as the response. Model specification in INLA is done by translating the linear predictor into a formula and defining the latent SPDE component. The Matérn SPDE is created with inla.spde2.pcmatern(), and the latent field enters the formula through terms like f(s, model = spde).

To connect the data support (coarse cells) to the mesh representation, we build projection matrices and assemble the stacks. Spatially, the key object is the projection matrix (e.g., A.m from regions to mesh nodes, and A.pr from mesh nodes to prediction points). In practice, we pass these matrices to inla.stack() through its A= argument, and we build separate stacks for estimation and prediction, which are then combined into a single object (e.g., stk.full).

Finally, we fit the model with inla(). The stacked data are provided with inla.stack.data(), and the corresponding projection matrix is passed through control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(...), compute = TRUE) so INLA returns fitted values and predictions. Predictions are retrieved using inla.stack.index() to select the prediction rows, and then extracting the posterior summaries from res$summary.linear.predictor. Fixed-effect summaries are obtained from res$summary.fixed, and the same workflow extends naturally from the univariate spatial example to the multivariate and spatio-temporal settings by changing the model formula and the stack/projection structure.

3 Spatial disaggregation example

In this section, we illustrate spatial disaggregation by improving the resolution of PM2.5 concentrations in Portugal from 10 km to 2 km. We used monthly air quality reanalysis data for Portugal provided by the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) (Inness et al. 2019), a high-resolution product developed by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). This publicly accessible dataset, available at https://ads.atmosphere.copernicus.eu/datasets/cams-europe-air-quality-reanalyses, integrates satellite observations and auxiliary information to get estimations of air pollution levels at a relatively coarse resolution.

3.1 PM2.5 disaggregation model

The main objective of this model is to perform spatial disaggregation by increasing the resolution from \(0.1^\circ\) to \(0.02^\circ\), which corresponds approximately to a change from 10 km to 2 km, using INLA. We also include elevation as a high-resolution covariate to help explain local variation in PM2.5 and improve the disaggregation. The model assumes the existence of a latent continuous spatial process for PM2.5 that is observed only through aggregated measurements. Specifically,

\[\begin{equation} \text{pm}_{2.5}(\mathbf{s}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{elevation}(\mathbf{s}) + z(\mathbf{s}) + e(\mathbf{s}), \tag{8} \end{equation}\] where \(\beta_0\) is an intercept and \(\beta_1\) is the regression coefficient associated with elevation. The term \(z(\mathbf{s})\) represents a spatially structured random effect, modeled as a zero mean Gaussian process with a Matérn covariance function, and \(e(\mathbf{s})\) is an unstructured error term, modeled as a zero mean Gaussian process that is independent across space. The link between the latent field and the areal observations is defined through Equations (1), (2), and (3). Inference is then performed using the projection (aggregation) matrix described in Section 2.3.

3.2 Data acquisition and preprocessing

In this section, we describe how to obtain the PM2.5 dataset and the covariate information used in our model. We first show how to download and preprocess the air pollution data, and then we explain how to collect and preprocess elevation data for modeling using INLA.

Observed particulate matter values in Portugal

To download PM2.5 data, we need to create an account on the Atmospheric Data Store (ADS), accept the terms and conditions, and obtain the “Licence to use Copernicus Products.” After setup, the data can be downloaded using the Python API. More details on setting up the API are available at https://ads.atmosphere.copernicus.eu/how-to-api. In our request, the argument variable = ["particulate_matter_2.5um"] selects PM2.5 concentrations, model = ["ensemble"] specifies the ensemble product, level = ["0"] indicates the surface level, type = ["validated_reanalysis"] requests the validated reanalysis product, and year = ["2019"] and month = ["01"] restrict the download to January 2019.

After downloading and unzipping the data, we use the terra package to read the nc file. NetCDF (Network Common Data Form) files are widely used for storing multi-dimensional scientific data, such as climate or GIS datasets, because they are self-describing, portable, and efficient for large arrays. The original dataset contains hourly samples for the 31 days of January 2019, totaling 744 observations. Since our focus is on identifying mean trends, we calculated the average PM2.5 concentration for each location. As the original data covers the entire European continent, we cropped the spatial extent to focus specifically on Portugal. To provide better geographical context in our visualizations, we also included the administrative boundaries of Portugal and Spain for clear regional identification using packages rnaturalearth and sf. Finally for plotting we used ggplot2, tidyterra and viridis packages.

# Define the squared study region
sq <- ext(-9.65, -6.05, 36.85, 42.25)

# Read the dataset and compute mean value (From source)
r <- rast("data/cams.eaq.vra.ENSa.pm2p5.l0.2019-01.nc")
r_mean <- app(r, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
r_sq <- crop(r_mean, sq)
df <- as.data.frame(r_sq, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
df <- df[order(df$y, df$x), ]
names(df) <- c("longitude", "latitude", "pm2p5")
write.csv(df, "data/pm2p5_portugal.csv", row.names = FALSE)

To simplify replication and avoid the ADS download and NetCDF preprocessing steps, we provide the preprocessed dataset as pm2p5_portugal.csv, which contains the processed PM2.5 values in CSV format. Figure (2) shows the spatial distribution of mean PM2.5 over Portugal for January 2019. Higher concentrations are observed along the western coast. The map is provided on the original CAMS grid (about 0.1\(^\circ\), roughly 10 km), which is relatively coarse for local-scale interpretation; we therefore target a finer resolution of 0.02\(^\circ\) (approximately 2 km) using spatial disaggregation.

# Define the squared study region
sq <- ext(-9.65, -6.05, 36.85, 42.25)

# Read dataset from preprocess file
df <- read.csv("data/pm2p5_portugal.csv")
r_sq <- rast(df[, c("longitude", "latitude", "pm2p5")])

# Get Portugal and Spain borders
boundary <- ne_countries(scale="medium", returnclass="sf") |>
  subset(admin %in% c("Portugal", "Spain")) |>
  st_transform(4326)

# Plot PM2.5 contamination and boundary countries
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = r_sq) +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "red") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "PM2.5") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9)
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(xmin(sq), xmax(sq)),
           ylim = c(ymin(sq), ymax(sq)),
           expand = FALSE)

Figure 2: Mean PM2.5 concentration in Portugal during January 2019. Country boundaries for Portugal and Spain are overlaid for geographic reference.

Covariates

We incorporate high resolution elevation data, at approximately \(60\)m resolution, from the EuroDEM product maintained by EuroGeographics (EuroGeographics and European NMCAs 2023) that is available in the following website https://www.mapsforeurope.org/datasets/euro-dem. Elevation is included as a covariate to relate PM2.5 concentrations with changes in altitude and to improve the explanatory power of the spatial disaggregation model across the study region. The data do not identify how the field varies within an input cell, so the fine-scale detail depends on the covariates and on the smoothness of the field (Suen et al. 2026). In our case, removing elevation changes the predictions little (RMSE of 0.015 \(\mu\)g/m\(^3\) and maximum difference of 0.14 \(\mu\)g/m\(^3\)), and we expect covariates to matter more where local effects are stronger.

EuroDEM is provided at very fine resolution and covers all Europe, so we first crop it to the study region, keeping a small margin so that all grid cells are fully covered, and then reproject and aggregate it. To avoid downloading the full product, we provide this preprocessed version, called eurodemc.tif.

r <- rast("data/eurodem.tif")
# The coordinates of this file are stored in arc-seconds
r_sub <- crop(r, ext(as.vector(extend(sq, 0.07)) * 3600))
ext(r_sub) <- as.vector(ext(r_sub)) / 3600
crs(r_sub) <- "EPSG:4326"
# Keep a margin of 0.05 degrees around the study region
target <- rast(extend(sq, 0.05), res = 5 / 3600, crs = "EPSG:4326")
r_map <- project(r_sub, target, method = "bilinear")
r_ag <- aggregate(r_map, fact = 2, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
r_ag <- round(r_ag, 1)
names(r_ag) <- "eurodem"
writeRaster(r_ag, "data/eurodemc.tif", overwrite = TRUE, datatype = "FLT4S",
            gdal = "COMPRESS=LZW")

This preprocessing took about 4 seconds on a laptop with an Intel Core Ultra 9 285H (16 cores) and 63.5 GB of RAM, running Windows 11, without parallelization. After preprocessing, Figure (3) shows the resulting elevation raster over Portugal, with values reported in meters.

# Reading elevation dataset
r_crop <- rast("data/eurodemc.tif")
r_crop[is.na(r_crop)] <- 0

ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = r_crop) +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "red") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Elevation (m)") +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9)
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(xmin(sq), xmax(sq)),
           ylim = c(ymin(sq), ymax(sq)),
           expand = FALSE)

Figure 3: EuroDEM elevation raster over Portugal (meters), cropped to the study region and used as a covariate in the disaggregation model.

3.3 INLA modeling

After obtaining the PM2.5 dataset and the elevation covariate, we need to prepare several additional objects before fitting the disaggregation model with INLA. We proceed in the following order. First, we define the input grid, build the spatial mesh, and create the prediction locations on the finer resolution grid. Next, we align the elevation covariate with both the input grid and the prediction grid. We then specify the SPDE in the spatial mesh, construct the projection matrices and assemble the corresponding INLA stacks for estimation and prediction. Finally, we fit the model with INLA and summarize the results, and we compare the coarse input field with the disaggregated predictions on the finer scale.

Input grid, mesh, and prediction locations

The first step in the disaggregation workflow is to construct an input grid that matches the support of the observed data. Using the dataframe df, we build a squared grid as an sf object with the same spatial extent and dimensions as the original dataset. The second step is to build a spatial mesh that is finer than the initial resolution of the data, as shown on the left side of Figure (4). We build it in UTM zone 29N (EPSG:32629), in kilometers, so that the spatial range is interpretable. A hexagonal lattice gives triangles of nearly equal size and shape, st_buffer() extends the inner mesh 10 km beyond the study region so that all input cells are covered, and fm_extensions() adds an outer mesh that reduces boundary effects. The mesh should be finer than the input cells and small compared with the spatial range, but it does not need to be as fine as the elevation data, because that would add runtime for only a small improvement. In our case, going from an edge length of 5 km to 3 km increased the fit time from about 0.3 to 1.3 minutes, while the predictions changed very little (RMSE of 0.010 \(\mu\)g/m\(^3\)).

Finally, we define the prediction points on the \(0.02^\circ\) grid. Setting \(\texttt{spf}=5\) increases the resolution within each original cell by a factor of \(5 \times 5 = 25\), as illustrated on the right side of Figure (4). We obtain these locations, the centers of the finer grid cells, with fm_pixels(). We evaluate the latent field at these centers, which approximates its average over each finer cell.

# Initial squared grid
map <- st_as_sf(st_make_grid(sq, n = c(length(unique(df$longitude)),
                               length(unique(df$latitude)))))
st_geometry(map) <- "geometry"
st_crs(map) <- "EPSG:4326"

# Spatial mesh in UTM zone 29N, in kilometers
crs_km <- fm_crs("+proj=utm +zone=29 +datum=WGS84 +units=km +no_defs")
map_km <- st_transform(map, crs_km)
inner <- st_buffer(st_union(map_km), 10)

hexpts <- fm_hexagon_lattice(
  bnd = inner,
  edge_len = 5
)

mesh <- fm_mesh_2d(
  loc = hexpts,
  boundary = fm_extensions(inner, convex = c(10, 150), concave = c(10, 150),
                           resolution = c(100, 170)),
  max.edge = c(10, 50),
  crs = crs_km
)

# prediction points

spf <- 5 # spatial factor
def <- abs(unique(df$latitude)[2]-unique(df$latitude)[1])/(2*spf)

dpdf_sf <- fm_pixels(
  fm_transform(mesh, crs = "EPSG:4326"),
  dims = c(length(unique(df$longitude)), length(unique(df$latitude)))*spf,
  xlim = c(xmin(sq) + def, xmax(sq) - def),
  ylim = c(ymin(sq) + def, ymax(sq) - def),
  format = "sf"
)
dp_km <- st_transform(dpdf_sf, crs_km)
dp <- st_coordinates(dp_km)

# Plots
corner <- st_bbox(c(xmin = -9.7, ymin = 36.8, xmax = -9.4, ymax = 37.1), crs = 4326)
corner <- st_bbox(st_transform(st_as_sfc(corner), crs_km))
xl <- c(corner[["xmin"]], corner[["xmax"]])
yl <- c(corner[["ymin"]], corner[["ymax"]])
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), pty = "s")
plot(mesh, xlim = xl, ylim = yl, asp = 1, main = "")
plot(map_km$geometry, add = TRUE, border = "red", lwd = 2)

plot(map_km$geometry, border = "red", lwd = 2, xlim = xl, ylim = yl, asp = 1)
plot(st_geometry(dp_km), add = TRUE, col = "blue", pch = 20, cex = 0.6)

Figure 4: Spatial discretization for disaggregation. Original grid support is shown in red. A portion of the triangulated mesh is shown in black (left), and prediction points for spf=5 are shown in blue (right).

Elevation covariate on input and prediction grids

To incorporate this covariate within the disaggregation framework, we align its spatial support with both the original CAMS grid and the high-resolution prediction grid. For this purpose, we use the exactextractr package, which provides efficient tools for extracting and summarizing raster values over polygonal features. We compute the mean elevation within each 0.1\(^\circ\) CAMS input cell and within each 0.02\(^\circ\) prediction cell, so that the covariate is available at the same spatial support as both the observed and predicted quantities. Figure (5) illustrates the resulting elevation covariate over Portugal, with the input grid shown on the left and the prediction grid shown on the right.

# Extract elevation values in the original dataset
map$elev <- exact_extract(r_crop, map, "mean", progress = FALSE)

# Create the prediction dataset in sf format
map_pred <- st_as_sf(st_make_grid(sq, n = c(length(unique(df$longitude)),
                               length(unique(df$latitude)))*spf))
st_crs(map_pred) <- "EPSG:4326"

# Extract elevation values in the prediction dataset
map_pred$elev <- exact_extract(r_crop, map_pred, "mean", progress = FALSE)

# Common color scale for both panels
lims <- range(c(map$elev, map_pred$elev))

# Plot elevation in the input grid
p1 <- ggplot(map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = elev), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Elevation (m)", limits = lims) +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "red") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-10, -6), ylim = c(36.5, 42.5),
           expand = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
  )

# Plot elevation in the prediction grid
p2 <- ggplot(map_pred) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = elev), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Elevation (m)", limits = lims) +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "red") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-10, -6), ylim = c(36.5, 42.5),
           expand = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
  )

p1 + p2 + plot_layout(guides = "collect")

Figure 5: Elevation over Portugal on the input grid (left) and the prediction grid (right), with country boundaries for reference.

SPDE specification, projection matrices and INLA stacks

To fit the model described in Equation (8), we use the triangulated mesh defined before in Section 3.3. We then construct the SPDE representation on this mesh, using penalized complexity priors (Fuglstad et al. 2019) for the range \(\rho\) and the standard deviation \(\sigma\) of the field, with \(P(\rho < 50 \text{ km}) = 0.5\) and \(P(\sigma > 5) = 0.01\), and build the corresponding projection matrices that link the observation locations and the prediction points to the mesh nodes. To compute the matrix A.m as described in Section 2.3, we create a grid of points in each input cell and pass them to inla.spde.make.A(). The argument block indicates the cell of each point, and block.rescale = "sum" averages the values within each cell. In our case, with a \(20 \times 20\) grid in each of the 1,944 input cells, this takes about 4 seconds. Finally, we combine the response, covariates, and latent components into stacks, which are used to perform model estimation and prediction.

# Construct the SPDE in the spatial mesh
spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh, alpha = 2, constr = TRUE,
                            prior.range = c(50, 0.5),
                            prior.sigma = c(5, 0.01))

nv <- mesh$n # number of mesh nodes

# Grid of m x m points in each cell, then projected to UTM
m <- 20
cell_points <- function(cell) {
  b <- st_bbox(cell)
  dx <- (b[["xmax"]] - b[["xmin"]]) / m
  dy <- (b[["ymax"]] - b[["ymin"]]) / m
  as.matrix(expand.grid(x = b[["xmin"]] + dx * (seq_len(m) - 0.5),
                        y = b[["ymin"]] + dy * (seq_len(m) - 0.5)))
}
pts <- do.call(rbind, lapply(st_geometry(map), cell_points))
pts <- st_as_sf(data.frame(pts), coords = c("x", "y"), crs = "EPSG:4326")
pts <- st_coordinates(st_transform(pts, crs_km))

# Projection matrix from initial data to the triangulated mesh
A.m <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = pts,
                        block = rep(seq_len(nrow(map)), each = m^2),
                        block.rescale = "sum")

# Projection matrix from the mesh to the predicted points
A.pr <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = dp)

# Stack for estimation
stk.est <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = df$pm2p5),
  A = list(A.m, A.m, 1),
  effects = list(
    s = 1:nv,
    b0 = rep(1, nv),
    elev = map$elev/1000 # convert m to km
  ),
  tag = "y")

# Stack for prediction
stk.pred <- inla.stack(
  data = list(y = NA),
  A = list(A.pr, A.pr, 1),
  effects = list(
    s = 1:nv,
    b0 = rep(1, nv),
    elev = map_pred$elev/1000 # convert m to km
    ),
  tag = "y.pred")

# Stack for estimation and prediction
stk.full <- inla.stack(stk.est, stk.pred)

Model fitting with INLA

Now, we translate Equation (8) into an INLA formula, where the symbol ~ defines the linear predictor for the response \(y\). The term 0 + b0 adds an explicit intercept, with b0 being a column of ones included in the stack. The term elev represents elevation as a fixed effect, and f(s, model = spde) specifies the spatial random effect on the mesh using the SPDE model. We fit the model with inla() using the stacked data object stk.full, and set family = "gaussian" because \(y\) is continuous.

# INLA formula
form <- y ~ 0 + b0 + elev + f(s, model = spde)

# Fitting and prediction
res <- inla(
  formula=form,
  data = inla.stack.data(stk.full, spde = spde),
  family = "gaussian",
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk.full),
                           compute = TRUE, link = 1)
)

# Summary for the fixed effects
res$summary.fixed |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3) |>
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

The model fit took about 18 seconds on the laptop described in Section 3.2. Table (1) summarizes the posterior distributions of the fixed effects. The posterior mean of the intercept \(\beta_0\) is 8.22 \(\mu\)g/m\(^3\), which represents the PM2.5 level when elevation is zero. Its uncertainty is large (95% credible interval from 7.26 to 9.17 \(\mu\)g/m\(^3\)) because it is hard to separate from the long-range variation of the spatial field. The posterior credible interval for the elevation coefficient excludes zero, indicating a clear association between elevation and PM2.5. The posterior mean is \(-0.28\), implying that an increase of 1 km in altitude is associated with a decrease of about 0.28 \(\mu\)g/m\(^3\) in PM2.5. The posterior median of the spatial range is 403 km (95% credible interval from 247 to 682 km).

b0 8.215 0.485 7.263 8.215 9.168 8.215 0
elev -0.281 0.063 -0.404 -0.281 -0.159 -0.281 0

Input data and disaggregated predictions

Figure (6) compares the coarse input PM2.5 field (left) with the posterior mean predictions from the disaggregation model on the finer grid (right). The disaggregated surface provides a smoother and more detailed representation of spatial variability, while maintaining the main concentration levels and spatial patterns observed in the input data. We also notice that the range of the predicted surface is slightly wider than the range of the input data. This is an important advantage of the disaggregation approach, since it can reveal localized areas with higher or lower concentrations than suggested by the coarse grid, which can be useful for decision-makers.

# get indexes of the response variable
idx <- inla.stack.index(stk.full, 'y.pred')$data

# Input grid
map$pm2p5 <- df$pm2p5

# Prediction
map_pred$pm2p5 <- res$summary.linear.predictor[idx, "mean"]

# Common color scale for both panels
lims <- range(c(map$pm2p5, map_pred$pm2p5))

# Plot for input grid
p1 <- ggplot(map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = pm2p5), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "PM2.5", limits = lims) +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "red") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-10, -6), ylim = c(36.5, 42.5),
           expand = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
  )

# Plot for predictions
p2 <- ggplot(map_pred) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = pm2p5), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "PM2.5", limits = lims) +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, color = "red") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-10, -6), ylim = c(36.5, 42.5),
           expand = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 9),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 5.5, r = 5.5, b = 18, l = 5.5)
  )

# Combine plots
p1 + p2 + plot_layout(guides = "collect")

Figure 6: PM2.5 over Portugal on the input grid (left) and disaggregated predictions on the finer grid (right).

4 Conclusion and discussion

In this paper we have demonstrated how to perform spatial disaggregation with INLA. Using an application to PM2.5 data, we have shown how to formulate a spatial disaggregation model by assuming an underlying latent Gaussian field defined at a finer scale than the observed data. The observations are then treated as aggregated measurements of this latent field over larger spatial units. Within this framework, covariates are incorporated at the fine scale, allowing high-resolution information to capture local variation that would otherwise be obscured at coarser supports. The key practical component in the implementation is the projection matrix, which links the mesh representation of the latent field to the observed spatial units. By adopting the INLA–SPDE approach, we represent the latent field on a triangulated mesh which makes inference computationally efficient while still providing Bayesian uncertainty quantification.

In the application presented, we disaggregate PM2.5 over Portugal from the CAMS \(0.1^\circ\) grid to \(0.02^\circ\), and we include elevation (EuroDEM) as a covariate to relate pollution levels to altitude and improve the spatial interpretation. This framework is based on the implementation developed in (Moraga et al. 2017). This approach can be extended to multivariate settings by jointly disaggregating several air pollutants, and spatio-temporal settings to estimate variables at higher resolutions both in space and in time. For example, (Rodriguez Avellaneda et al. 2026) utilized a multivariate setting using the Linear Model of Coregionalization (LMC), to jointly disaggregate PM2.5, PM10, and ozone over Portugal using the same CAMS product (Inness et al. 2019). (Rodriguez Avellaneda and Moraga 2026) extended this approach to the spatio-temporal setting and disaggregated Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) at 550 nm over India using the EAC4 reanalysis from ECMWF (Inness et al. 2019). In that example, they refined the spatial resolution from \(0.75^\circ\) to \(0.25^\circ\) and the temporal resolution from 3-hourly to hourly, producing spatio-temporal predictions at intermediate time points that were not available in the original product.

The spatial model presented in this paper considers Gaussian responses, where the aggregation is linear in the latent field and the observations can be linked to the field directly through the projection matrix. More general response variables, for example Poisson counts such as disease cases over administrative units, are more challenging because the expected count in a region is the integral of an exponential function of the latent field, which is nonlinear in the field. The inlabru package (Lindgren et al. 2024) addresses this type of model by fitting INLA iteratively to a linearized version of the predictor, and (Suen et al. 2026) use this approach for the disaggregation of aggregated counts. The accuracy argument given in the Introduction does not extend to these non-Gaussian settings, particularly with sparse counts or binary data, where INLA results should be checked against MCMC. On the spatio-temporal side, recent work has proposed efficient spatial disaggregation methods for spatio-temporal datasets (Gaedke-Merzhäuser et al. 2025), while the spatio-temporal model in (Rodriguez Avellaneda and Moraga 2026) goes one step further by disaggregating not only in space but also in time. A further direction is to combine these ideas and build multivariate spatio-temporal disaggregation models that jointly downscale multiple variables across space and time, and that can handle variables observed on different spatial or temporal supports within a single coherent framework (Zhong et al. 2025).

Overall, this paper presents a practical disaggregation workflow based on latent Gaussian fields and the INLA–SPDE framework, which scales well and can be adapted to spatial, multivariate, and spatio-temporal settings. Although we focus on an air pollution application, the same framework applies to other continuous variables observed on coarse spatial supports, where the goal is to recover the underlying process at a finer resolution with uncertainty quantification. Examples include remotely sensed or reanalysis products such as land-surface temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, sea-surface temperature, and vegetation indices, as well as other environmental exposures available as gridded averages (Gómez-Rubio and Palmí-Perales 2019; Forlani et al. 2020; Moraga and Baker 2022).
